_about: The order in which Liebermann prints the clauses of law codes whose order is not simply numerical (Alfred keeps Thorpe’s and Schmid’s numbers out of order; Epilog, Rubriken and the like are labels, not numbers). tools/laws-from-database.py keeps these codes in this order and never sorts them by number, and warns if a rebuild comes out in a different order. law.html and lawcode.html show the notes, each as an ‘Editor’s note’: 'notes' on a clause's page, 'codeNotes' in the whole-code views just before the clause named in 'before'. 'codeIntros' is the text behind the ‘About the numbering’ button on a law code’s page (HTML).

Liebermann gives this heading no label in his margin (Gesetze I, p. 17); his Wörterbuch cites it as “Af Insc” (s.vv. geceosan, swicdome, þes) and once as “Af Rb Pro” (s.v. is). The label “Af Rb Inscr.” follows his usage for other headings.

Að.2: Liebermann prints this passage as Að 2, the second chapter of Að, following the manuscripts in which it continues the Mercian oath (Gesetze I, p. 464). Whitelock and Rabin follow Cambridge, Corpus Christi College, MSS 201 and 190, which give it a heading of its own and go straight on into Hadbot; Rabin’s ‘On Priests’ Oaths’ begins here. The Textus Roffensis (H) has it before Að 1.

Af.title: About the numbering
Af.html:
The clause divisions and citation numbers used here are Liebermann’s. Each of the ‘clauses’ included in this database is, in Liebermann’s terms, a ‘chapter’ (Capitel), divided further at times into paragraphs (Paragraphen), so that a single ‘chapter’ of law with three ‘paragraphs’ will appear as (for example) the sequence Af 4, Af 4.1, Af 4.2.

Liebermann did not himself devise this system. He took it over from the editions of Reinhold Schmid (1832; 2nd edn 1858) and Benjamin Thorpe (1840), and kept strictly to the established numbers even where he thought them wrong. This deference to his editorial predecessors was motivated, at least in part, by a desire that earlier, established citations should not become obsolete. Of Alfred’s laws he wrote that he would otherwise have begun a new chapter at, for example, 5.5, 9.2, 18.1 and 40.2 (‘sonst hätt ich z.B. mit Af 5,5. 9,2. 18,1. 40,2. ein neues Kapitel begonnen’, Gesetze III, 40). For the same reason the citations between 25.1 and 31.1 are not in numerical order (see the note at 29).

Modern commentators have often chafed under this system (see e.g. Wormald, The Making of English Law, p. 22). Stefan Jurasinski and Lisi Oliver’s now-standard edition (The Laws of Alfred, 2021) renumbers Alfred’s and Ine’s laws from §5 on, and alters the division between prologue and code. Their edition gives Liebermann’s numbers in square brackets with an L, so that their §6 is Liebermann’s 5.5, written ‘6 [L5.5]’. The newer numbers, which must be taken as standard, appear here in grey bubbles wherever their edition is cited. Liebermann’s now obsolete numbering is retained as the structure of the Domboc for technical reasons: to ensure that links to his Wörterbuch and cross-references to scholarship can function. See also Editorial Principles.

codeIntroductions.Cn 1018: The code of 1018 is the record of the agreement between Danes and English made at Oxford in 1018 and recorded in the Chronicle, at which all undertook to keep the law of Edgar. It survives only in CCCC 201, a collection associated with Wulfstan; it was drafted by Wulfstan. Whitelock identified it and connected it with the Oxford meeting, and Kennedy has edited it as a self-contained legal text. Liebermann did not edit it as an independent code, but prints it partially and discontinuously as the ‘D’ text of VI Æthelred. It is essentially a version of Wulfstan’s Enham legislation of 1008, close in wording to VI Æthelred but nearer in order to V and to Cnut’s later code. It drops most of the secular provisions, adds a clause from Edgar on just judgement with a new tariff of fines, and ends with material from the appendix to VI Æthelred. Its legal content is slight and its exhortation abundant; Wormald sees it as a provisional statement that Wulfstan later built into I–II Cnut. (Wormald, MEL, pp. 131–2, 334, 346–7, 355)
codeIntroductions.Ps Cn for: A set of forest laws that claims to have been issued by Cnut in person with the counsel of his leading men. It is a forgery produced in the twelfth century, perhaps during the reign of Henry II (r. 1154–89). Liebermann suggested 1130–1217, and perhaps c. 1185, for the date of its composition; its only witnesses are early modern, all of the late sixteenth century or after. Some of its clauses are based on the Instituta Cnuti; original clauses may reflect twelfth-century forest laws. The code as a whole may stand as an attempt to give legal and historical legitimacy to unpopular royal forest laws. Liebermann also edited this code separately (Über Pseudo-Cnuts Constitutiones de foresta, 1894).
codeIntroductions.Abt: The earliest surviving English law code, written in Old English and attributed to Æthelberht of Kent (d. 616). Its ascription to Æthelberht rests on Bede, and on the rubric in the Textus Roffensis (the only manuscript containing this code), which places the laws in Augustine’s time. Wormald sets aside that rubric and with it the need for a date before 604 (Liebermann dated the code 601–4); he suggests instead a date in or soon after 614, when Kentish churchmen attended Chlothar II’s Council of Paris. The text is a neatly ordered tariff of compensations, running from the Church and king through nobles, freemen, injuries and women to the unfree, couched in very simple syntax; Wormald regards most of it as existing custom written down rather than new law. He stresses that the clause divisions of modern editions, including Liebermann’s, have no basis in the manuscript (see Wormald, MEL, pp. 93–101, 244–5, 252; and see Oliver, pp. 3–51).
codeIntroductions.Erc: No laws of Earconberht of Kent (640–64) survive. The only witness is Bede, who reports that Æthelberht’s grandson ordered idols to be abandoned and the Lenten fast to be kept. Wormald mentions the notice only in passing, contrasting these explicitly Christian measures with the largely secular content of Æthelberht’s code as an argument for the latter’s early date (Wormald, MEL, pp. 93–4).
codeIntroductions.Hl: The second Kentish code, issued in the names of Hlothhere (673–85) and his nephew Eadric (685–6), who ruled Kent jointly for a period. In its prologue, Hlothhere and Eadric are adding judgements (domas) to the established law (æ) of their predecessors. The vocabulary of this code is close to Æthelberht’s, but its sentences are more involved. The code deals with a number of matters of legal procedure, and ends with rules for trading in London, a sign perhaps of growing urban commerce. It survives only in the Textus Roffensis (see Wormald, MEL, pp. 93, 101–3, 245; and see Oliver, pp. 117–23).
codeIntroductions.Wi: The last of the Kentish codes, issued (according to its prologue) by Wihtred (690/1–725) with his councillors, among them Archbishop Berhtwald of Canterbury and the bishop of Rochester. Its prologue gives both a place and a date by month and regnal year, which can be read as 6 September 695. Most of the code deals with the standing of the Church and clergy: its freedom from tribute, unlawful unions, several of the Ten Commandments made enforceable by the king, and how clerics of different grades may clear themselves of charges. It ends with clauses on slaying or seizing thieves that seem to be borrowed from Ine. Because of its ecclesiastical content, exact dating and change of vocabulary, Wormald raises the possibility that it began as a Latin synodal decree later put into English. It survives only in the Textus Roffensis (see Wormald, MEL, pp. 93, 101–3, 245–7; and see Oliver, pp. 147–50). For more on similarities and borrowings between Wihtred’s and Ine’s codes, see Jurasinski and Oliver, pp. 25, 28–9, 43–51.
codeIntroductions.In Cn:
The Instituta Cnuti aliorumque regum Anglorum (Liebermann’s title) is a Latin translation of Old English laws made soon after the Conquest, for readers who knew Latin but not English. Most of it translates the laws of Cnut; it also draws on Alfred and Ine, II Edgar, and the short texts on rank and oaths (Mirce, Að, Hadbot, Geþyncðo, Grið), and about a dozen chapters translate Old English texts now lost.

Liebermann does not print it as one text. He prints each passage once, as a Latin column beside the law it translates, and here gives in full only what has no Old English source; the other entries in this list point to where the passage stands (“o. S. 343–47”, above, pp. 343–47). To read the whole work in its own order, use Instituta Cnuti, read in order, which puts the passages back together from all the places they are printed.

Books I and II follow the numbering of I and II Cnut (In Cn II 54 translates II Cnut 54); the translator’s additions carry letters (I 12c). Liebermann’s bold, spaced and smaller type, and his round brackets, show how the translation differs from its source: see Liebermann’s kinds of type.

Manuscripts. The full text (to III 64) is in H (Textus Roffensis), Rl, T and Cb; the short text (ending in III 44) in Di and the copies inserted into Henry of Huntingdon’s Historia (Ip Hunt: Lb, S, Pl, Ct, Jo, Va and others). O’Brien shows that Rl is a copy of H, that Cb is a reviser’s text, and adds two manuscripts Liebermann did not use. See the manuscripts of the Instituta.

Liebermann’s edition of this text has been criticised by Bruce O’Brien (Anglo-Norman Studies 25 (2003), 177–97) for errors of transcription, a mistaken view of the manuscripts, and for marking only the larger changes the translator made and none of his omissions. No new edition has yet appeared.
codeIntroductions.VI Atr:
VI Æthelred is one of the two law codes associated with the meeting of the king’s council at Enham on 16 May 1008; the other is V Æthelred. Its place among Archbishop Wulfstan’s writings is less clear-cut than that of V Æthelred. It survives in Old English and in a Latin version, VI Æthelred, Latin paraphrase, which was probably made slightly later than the Old English. Both are additions to London, British Library, Cotton MS Claudius A.iii (Liebermann’s K), a pontifical that Wulfstan used early in his career, and the Latin ends with a clause naming Wulfstan as the one who set these decrees down in writing (VI Atr Lat 40.2).

Many of its clauses resemble those of V Æthelred, though in a different order. VI Æthelred also elaborates on them in ways that point to Wulfstan’s later works, above all in putting the clauses on Church law first and in its fuller list of the dues owed to the Church. It is therefore likely that VI Æthelred is not an official enactment but a draft of V Æthelred, in which Wulfstan tried out policies that would later become regular features of his legislation (Rabin, Old English Legal Writings: Wulfstan, p. xxvii).
codeIntroductions.VI Atr Lat:
This is the Latin version of VI Æthelred, which Liebermann heads ‘Paraphrase aus dem Anfange des XI. Jahrhunderts’ (a paraphrase from the beginning of the eleventh century). It was probably made slightly later than the Old English text. Both survive as additions to London, British Library, Cotton MS Claudius A.iii (Liebermann’s K), a pontifical that Archbishop Wulfstan used early in his career. Its final clause (VI Atr Lat 40.2) names Wulfstan, archbishop of York, as the one who set these decrees down in writing.

VI Æthelred is one of the two law codes associated with the meeting of the king’s council at Enham in 1008; the other is V Æthelred. Many of its clauses resemble those of V Æthelred, in a different order, but they are elaborated in ways that point to Wulfstan’s later works, especially in putting Church law first and in a fuller list of the dues owed to the Church. VI Æthelred is therefore likely not an official enactment but a draft of V Æthelred, in which Wulfstan tried out policies that would later become regular features of his legislation (Rabin, Old English Legal Writings: Wulfstan, p. xxvii).

Liebermann prints the Latin beside the Old English and labels each Latin sentence with the numbers of the Old English clauses it renders. In his edition, Latin set in smaller type corresponds exactly to the Old English (‘Kleingedrucktes entspricht dem Angelsächsischen genau’, Gesetze I, p. 247); the difference of type is not yet shown here.
